chapter: Radio, theaters and early dance forms
title: WWL radio, listeners, and a Natchez gambling-joint dance job
summary: DeDroit describes his Sunday WWL program, radio's reach, and playing at out-of-town spots such as Natchez where a gambling operator paid for his band.

story.theme_name: Radio and television work: staff jobs, shows and broadcasts
story.community_name: Working radio and television: network shows, studio staffs, talk-show bands

blocks.x: I was curious to know if you felt that, actually, you did go around the country and other places. Yes. Did you feel that you were really ahead of the trends coming from New Orleans, that they discovered a lot of things just a lot later and picked them up, things that had been done a long time before here, like when you were a kid or just coming up in music. And that it just took the rest of the country a long time to discover what was going on here. I think that New Orleans music had an

impression on it, because we used to play on radio, you know. I did a program every Sunday on WWL, and I got plenty of fan mail. When was this? Do you remember? Approximately. That was after Suburban Gardens, and the public's house closed in the early 40s. It was in the 40s. I see. Because I worked steady all the time. And one night I came out of the jazz club. I went on the board of the jazz club. I would talk about it because Miss Moe told me that when I counted the ballots, I didn't have one dissenting vote, which is quite a compliment, you know, because I had opposition for a new member of the board. And they liked me so much. And they used to introduce me every Sunday, that there'd be monotonous. One Sunday they introduced me to the audience, and I wasn't there. I was, you know, when I come out, they said, oh, there he is. Give me a big answer. But I, so I was in the men's room, and a man says, you don't know me at all, Johnny. He said, you, the reason why, perhaps the reason why I'm here. He says, when I was a youngster, and you'd come on the air at WWL, he said, I'd get my drums up and I'd play with you. It made me feel good. There's a man, you know, he, radio was far-reaching. I'll tell you why. Because when I was making the trip over to Biloxi, boy you had to wear khaki clothes and leggings and you'd have an average of five flats to get over there. You'd take a boat and then you'd row through the woods, the chef wrote, finished at Chef, and then you had to get a ferry. And I'm in a place getting gasoline, and a little bit of pump, they rolled it out, and then I hear Ray McNamara playing along. He's out there with the squirrels, you know what I mean? So I was, radio, it's everybody. I used to play in pieces, I never thought I existed. Like, you ever hear of Pankerville? Pankerville. Pankerville. Shortbread town. It's the river they have on, Pasooma, isn't it? Somewhere out there in the country. Yeah, I used to get there. They heard me, and I go there, and it's a nice nightclub, you know, nice people. I played in places when I see the outside, I said, they can't be, they can't afford this band. I go in and I say, is there a dance here tonight? I say, yeah. Well I'm Johnny E. Drighton, the ball is, Johnny O'Brien. And when the people come in, they're all dressed up, nice people. I play nice. I think, how can they do it? I don't know. I used to play in Natchez, this is the truth. I said, Mr. Junkin, how can you pay this band? We don't have anybody here. He said, John, let me worry about it. He had a gambling joint in the back then, he was taking their money. My saxophone player, Franzella, was great too. He made so many passes, he said, come here John, get the saxophone player, I don't want to play sax, I'll have to take my money. So I said, Franzella, come out of that damn job. He said, well, my woman, I said, you're going to play saxophone and stay out of the game with me. That's all. Because it wasn't so much that Franzella was winning, everybody was betting on Franzella, making passes. So then I found out how, but they were building the roads up there on Natchez. And Mr. Junkin, he owned a lot of gravel pits or something like that. And he put up a crude thing to give them the workers and the entertainment, because there was nothing in that nature, you know. So he brought my band. I said, look at that, and they paid me. I look at the game, nobody coming in. They'd dance, maybe take a drink, but it wasn't a dance. It was where you have a crowd that paid at the door to dance. But he was making it.
